description: Lists every file open in ByteRipper: its id (pass it as `document` to the other tools — never show it to the person), `label` (what to call it to the person: the file's name, told apart from another of the same name), `link` for a file on disk (the label as a Markdown link that brings it forward in ByteRipper — write it where you name the file), name, path, size, whether it has unsaved edits, and where it is — pane A or B of a tab, or a part opened over its parent file ("part", with the parent's id, the bytes of the parent it came from, and `decoded` — what the part's bytes are to those: `LZMA`, `XOR 77`, `Read-only`…, absent for a plain copy — and `keeps_offsets`, whether byte n of the part is byte n of the source). A part is read, searched and analysed by every tool as a file of its own, from address 0, in its decoded form, and its tool panel is its own. The document the reader is in comes first and is marked `focused`. Ids last as long as the file stays open.
name: documents
title: Open documents

description: What the person at ByteRipper is looking at and pointing to: the document they are in, the caret, the selection (null when there is only a caret), and the bytes on screen. Call it when they say "this", "here" or "what I selected". In a comparison of two files it also names the other one, which scrolls with this one.
name: focus
title: Where the reader is

description: Reads bytes of an open document as it is now, unsaved edits included. `format`: "hex" (default) gives rows of 16 bytes with their address and text, as the dump shows them; "ascii" a string with "." for bytes that are not printable; "utf16le" the bytes decoded as UTF-16LE text; "u8", "u16", "u32", "u64" a list of unsigned integers in hex, little-endian unless `endian` is "big". At most 4096 bytes; a range running past the end of the file is cut there and says so.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

endian.description: For u16, u32 and u64. Default "little".

length.description: How many bytes. Default 256, at most 4096.

name: read
title: Read bytes

description: Shows a place in a document to the person: brings its tab forward, scrolls the dump to it and moves the caret there — selecting `length` bytes when `select` is true, which is the default when a length is given. It is a step of the navigation history, so the person's Back returns to where they were. Use it to point at what you are talking about.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

length.description: How many bytes the place is. Default 0: just the caret.

select.description: Select the bytes. Default: true when `length` is given.

name: reveal
title: Show bytes to the reader

description: Puts an annotation on a place in a file: a short `title` (what the bytes are), an optional `note` (why they matter, or what you found there), and the place — a `document` or a file `path`, with `offset` and `length`, or a UEFI `node` — whole, or with `offset` and `length` counted from the node's first byte: a `find_bytes` match with `node` is `node` and `node_offset`. It is listed in the Annotations window and drawn over the bytes — a dashed outline, the note when the person rests the pointer on them — whenever the file is on screen, now or after it is opened later; it is kept when the file closes. Use it both to show what bytes are while you explain them and to leave a result for the person to check — with `survey`, one on each file that matches. Whenever it is about bytes you have already annotated — a pointer and its target, a size and the stretch it names, a checksum and what it covers — annotate the other end first and pass its id in `related_to`: the person sees the relation and cannot otherwise. `reveal: true` also brings the place on screen, opening the file in a tab if it is not. In a part — a fragment panel — it goes to the file the part came out of, at the same bytes where the part keeps the file's addresses, otherwise at the bytes the part was decoded from; `from_part` says where it was in the part. A place in bytes that are not the file's own — what a compressed section decompresses to, a LENV block decoded, given as a node there or as a part of them — is kept there: the annotation answers `decoded` (the section or block, the range in its bytes, the `codecs`), the person's double-click opens those bytes in a fragment panel at the place, and the card shows the codecs as badges, so the title need not name them. A place in a module's code — a `function`, or an instruction `address`, in a Code panel given as `document` or in a module's image `node` of a dump with a stored analysis — is a code annotation: the person's double-click opens the module's Code panel at that function or instruction, the panel shows the note beside it, and the answer has `code`. Annotations go with `remove_annotations` or when the person clears them.

address.description: Or an instruction's Ghidra address in that code — the place is the instruction.

document.description: The document it is in. Default: the focused one.

function.description: A function of a module's code, by name or Ghidra entry address: annotate it in the Code panel `document`, or in the module at image `node` of the dump `document`.

node.description: Or the UEFI node it is about, e.g. "0.2.5" — inside a compressed section too.

note.description: A sentence or two: why they matter, or what was found. At most 600 characters.

offset.description: The first byte: in the document, or with `node` from the node's first byte.

path.description: Or the file it is in, by path, open or not.

related_to.description: Ids of annotations this one is about, e.g. ["a1"] for the target of a pointer. Give it whenever there is such an annotation.

reveal.description: Also bring the place on screen. Default false.

title.description: A few words: what the bytes are. At most 80 characters.

name: annotate
title: Annotate a place

description: The annotations made so far, oldest first — on every file, or on a `document` or a file `path`: id, the file's `path` (and its `document` id while it is open), `range` and/or `node`, `decoded` for a place in decompressed or decoded bytes, `title`, `note`, `related_to`, and `author: "person"` for one the person made by hand. Pages: `limit` is a ceiling — a page also stops before the answer passes the size bound and then says `truncated: "size"`; pass `next` back as `after` until it is null. A page asked for after the list changed is refused.

after.description: The `next` of the page before, to go on from where it stopped.

document.description: Only the annotations on this document's file.

limit.description: The most items one page holds — a ceiling: a page stops sooner when the answer would pass the size bound, and says so with `truncated: "size"`. Default 50, at most 200.

path.description: Only the annotations on this file.

name: annotations
title: List annotations

description: Removes annotations: the ones named in `ids`, or every one on a `document` or a file `path`, or — with `all` — every one. Relations to a removed annotation go with it.

document.description: Remove every annotation on this document's file.

path.description: Remove every annotation on this file.

name: remove_annotations
title: Remove annotations

description: Opens a file by path without putting it on screen, read-only, and returns its document id — for the tools that take `document` (`read`, `uefi_tree`, `uefi_find`…), but not for the ones that show things (`reveal`, `annotate`, panels); `show` puts it on screen. A file already open in a tab answers with that tab's id. The last eight are kept parsed; older ones are closed and opened again when asked for. A file changed on disk is read again and keeps its id.

path.description: An absolute path, or one starting with ~/.

name: open_dump
title: Open a dump in the background

description: Closes a document `open_dump` opened. Files open in a tab are the person's and are not closed.

document.description: The background document's id.

name: close_dump
title: Close a background dump

description: Opens a background document in a new tab — or brings forward the tab that already has the file — and shows `offset` there, selecting `length` bytes when given. Returns the on-screen document's id, which replaces the background one. Never opens into a pane that holds a file. A tab is a change of context: to look inside a node or a stretch of a dump that is already on screen, use `open_part`, which opens a panel in the same window instead.

document.description: The document's id.

length.description: How many bytes to select. Default 0.

offset.description: Where to show. Default: the start.

name: show
title: Put a dump on screen

description: Runs one tool that takes `document` (`uefi_find`, `uefi_node`, `uefi_at`, `read`…) on every file in `folder` (or in `paths`), opening each in the background, and returns the answers grouped by the value at `group_by` — a dotted path into the tool's answer, e.g. "total", "matches.0.start", "values.0", "chain.-1.name" (a negative index counts from the end). Each group: the value, how many files gave it, and up to ten of the files; the largest groups first. A file is named by its path from `root` — the `folder`, or the folder all the `paths` share — so files of one name in different subfolders are told apart, and `root` joined to the name is the path to open. Files a tool refused are listed under `failed`. Takes a while on many large images; reports progress. At most 200 files. Pages: `limit` is the most groups on one page, a ceiling — a page also stops before the answer passes the size bound and then says `truncated: "size"`; pass `next` back as `after`, with the same other arguments, until it is null. The next page is answered from the same run, not a new one. A group whose value is too large alone gives it as the start of its JSON text, marked `truncated: "item"`.

after.description: The `next` of the page before, to go on from where it stopped.

folder.description: A folder of dumps: files ending in .bin, .rom, .fd, .cap, .dump, .img, .scap.

group_by.description: Where in the answer the value to group by is. Default: the whole answer.

limit.description: The most items one page holds — a ceiling: a page stops sooner when the answer would pass the size bound, and says so with `truncated: "size"`. Default 20, at most 100.

paths.description: Files to survey, instead of a folder.

recursive.description: Look in subfolders too. Default false.

tool.description: The tool to run on each file.

name: survey
title: Ask one question of many dumps

description: The runs of bytes where `document` and `against` differ, in address order — compared at the same absolute offsets, unsaved edits included, as the window's A/B comparison compares. Never aligned: data that moved shows as one long run, not as a move. Runs closer than `merge_gap` matching bytes are one run; each has `start`, `end` (half-open), `length` and `differing_bytes`, which is less than `length` where matching bytes were merged in. `totals` count the whole range, whatever the page. Only bytes both files hold are compared: when the sizes differ, `tail` says where the longer file's extra bytes are, and they are not counted. With `structure` "auto" each run says `where` it is in `document`: the top-level area (region, volume, ME partition) and the deepest node that covers the run whole — a run across a boundary is placed at the node holding both sides, never split. Ids are those `uefi_node` and `me_tree` take; `where` is empty when nothing covers it. `summary: true` answers the areas instead, those with no differences too. Pages: `limit` is a ceiling — a page also stops before the answer passes the size bound, and then says `truncated: "size"`; pass `next` back as `after` until it is null. A page asked for after either document changed is refused. Reads only; nothing on screen moves.

after.description: The `next` of the page before, to go on from where it stopped.

against.description: The id of the document to compare it with, from `documents` or `open_dump`.

document.description: The first document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

end.description: The first byte after the range. Default: the end of the shorter file.

limit.description: The most items one page holds — a ceiling: a page stops sooner when the answer would pass the size bound, and says so with `truncated: "size"`. Default 100, at most 1000.

merge_gap.description: At most this many matching bytes between two runs make them one. Default 16; 0 merges nothing.

offset.description: Where the compared range starts, the same in both. Default 0x0.

structure.description: Place each run in the firmware's structure, or not. Default auto.

summary.description: Answer the areas of the image with their differences instead of the runs. Default false.

name: diff
title: Byte differences

description: Shows `document` and `against` to the person as a pair — A and B side by side, their differences coloured — in the window's own comparison. A pair already on screen is brought forward; a document alone in its tab gets the other beside it; otherwise the two open in a new tab, leaving the person's tabs as they are. Answers the ids of A and B as they are on screen (a background document gets a new one). Then `reveal_diff` walks the differences. A part (`open_part`), or anything never saved, has no file to open beside another: the two open as copies of their bytes in a new tab, and the answer says `copies` — an edit there reaches neither the documents nor a parent.

against.description: The document to show beside it, as B.

document.description: The document to show as A. Default: the focused one.

name: compare
title: Show two documents side by side

description: Moves both panes of a pair `compare` showed to the next or previous difference — the step the window's own difference arrows take, with the person's grouping of nearby differences — from `from`, or from the caret. A step of the navigation history, so the person's Back returns. Answers the difference, or `found: false` at the end. `document` is either side of the pair.

document.description: A or B of the pair. Default: the focused one.

from.description: Where to look from. Default: the caret.

name: reveal_diff
title: Show the next difference

description: Every place a text or a byte pattern occurs, in one of two scopes. Without `node`: the document's bytes as they are stored, with unsaved edits — the find bar's own search — in address order, `offset`/`end` limiting the range. With `node` (an id from `uefi_tree`, `uefi_find` or `uefi_at`, or "root" for the whole image): what the UEFI tree holds at and under that node — every container opened, every compressed section searched in what it decompresses to (nested ones too), a BIOS Guard update in its assembled region, a Lenovo LENV block stored XOR-encoded decoded — and only so: a compressed stream or an encoded block as stored is not searched, nor is an ME region. Opening everything takes a few seconds on a large image the first time; the same search of unchanged bytes again — a next page — is answered from the last one. A text the file holds only compressed is found this way and not the other. `text` is looked for as ASCII, as UTF-16LE, or both (`encoding`, default both), any case with `ignore_case`; `hex` is bytes, with `??` for a byte that may be anything ("24 ?? 4D 49"). Each match: the `encoding` that matched; without `node`, `start`, `end` (half-open file addresses) and `where` it is, as `diff` places a run; with `node`, in tree order, the `node` that holds it whole (as `uefi_tree` gives it) with `node_offset`, its `volume` and `volume_offset`, and `start`/`end` in the file — or, inside a compressed section, `in_compressed: true`, the `section` (open it with `open_part` part "decompressed") and `buffer_start`/`buffer_end` in what it decompresses to, which `uefi_node_data` reads — and `decoded` ("XOR 77") in a LENV block decoded. With `context`, a `preview` of the bytes around it — none, and `redacted: true`, in an area the flash map names MSDM, Password or Key. `total` counts every match; with `node`, `unread` lists the compressed sections that would not decompress. Matches do not overlap unless `overlapping`: "AA" in "AAAA" is two, or three with it. Pages: `limit` is a ceiling — a page also stops before the answer passes the size bound and says `truncated: "size"`; pass `next` back as `after` until it is null. With `survey`, which dumps of a folder hold a string.

after.description: The `next` of the page before, to go on from where it stopped.

context.description: Bytes before and after each match to show in `preview`. Default 0, at most 64.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

end.description: The first byte after the searched range. Default: the end. Not with `node`.

hex.description: Bytes to find, as hex pairs; `??` for any byte: "24 ?? 4D 49".

ignore_case.description: Letters in either case — ASCII letters of `text`. Default false.

limit.description: The most items one page holds — a ceiling: a page stops sooner when the answer would pass the size bound, and says so with `truncated: "size"`. Default 100, at most 1000.

node.description: Search what the UEFI tree holds at and under this node, decompressed and decoded; "root" for the whole image.

offset.description: Where the search of the document starts. Default 0x0. Not with `node`.

overlapping.description: Count matches that overlap one another. Default false.

text.description: A text to find. Give `text` or `hex`.

name: find_bytes
title: Find bytes or text

description: Opens a stretch of a document as a part of its own, in a fragment panel over its parent's tab — as Open Zone and the UEFI Structure panel's Open do — and answers its new `document` id. This is the way to open a node, compressed or not, or any stretch you want to read or edit: it keeps the person in the window they are in, with the parent showing behind the panel. A new tab is for switching to another context or for comparing two parts; `compare` opens one. The part's addresses start at 0, so two blocks at different addresses of two dumps compare with `diff` and `compare`; every tool that takes `document` works on it. Give `offset` and `length`, or `node` (with `part`) for a UEFI node: "all" (the default) or "body" for its bytes — a node inside a compressed section opens as what it decompressed to — "decompressed" for what a compressed section decompresses to, "decoded" for a Lenovo LENV block (or one of its entries) decoded, its XOR encoding removed. The part stays linked: edits to it stay in it until the person puts them back with Update in Parent, which for a decompressed node compresses them again. The answer says which `part` opened, and a LENV block opened without "decoded" comes with a `hint`. Asking again for a part that is already open raises its panel and answers `reused: true` with its `document` — not a second copy. `tool_panel` names the tool panel the part shows, null when none: `open_panel` with the part's `document` opens one on it. From then on the UEFI tools name the same node in the parent and the part (`counterpart`, `decoded_in`), and a call that names the parent while the focus is on the part answers with a `focus_note`. The new part takes the focus, so a call that leaves out `document` now goes to the part, and a node id belongs to the document it was listed on, the parent: give `document` (the `parent` of the answer) when you go on with that node. A part has its own tree, with its own ids: the parent's 0.3.4.1.2.5 is 0.0.5 in the decoded block. The parent must be on screen (`show` puts a background dump there). Closes with `close_dump` or by the person.

document.description: The parent's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

length.description: How many bytes the part is.

name.description: What the part is called. Default: the parent's name and what it is.

node.description: Instead of `offset` and `length`: a UEFI node's id.

offset.description: Where the part starts in the parent.

part.description: With `node`: the whole node, its body, what a compressed section decompresses to, or a LENV block decoded. Default "all".

name: open_part
title: Open a part

description: Every place in a firmware image that refers to an address or a GUID, in the file and inside its compressed sections, grouped by the FFS file each is in — so "which modules use this region" is one call. `guid` is written as usual and searched in its EFI byte order. `address` is a file address (or, with `relative_to` "region", an offset in the BIOS region) and is searched in the forms `forms` names: `bus` — where the BIOS region is mapped below 4 GiB, the region's end at 0x100000000, as 32 and 64 bits; `file` — the file address; `region` — the offset in the BIOS region; each little-endian, 32 bits. Address hits are chance as often as not in code: each says the `form` it matched, and none is hidden, but a shorter form is not listed apart where it only matched inside a longer one. `scope`: "all" (default), "raw" (the file as stored) or "compressed" (what the sections decompress to). Per file: `file` (its id), `name`, `guid`, `type`, `in_compressed`, and `hits` — `form`, `section` and `section_offset` in it, `file_start` where the hit has a file address. A hit in no FFS file is listed by the deepest `node` holding it. `total` counts the hits, `files` the groups. Pages: `limit` is a ceiling on files — a page also stops before the answer passes the size bound and says `truncated: "size"`; pass `next` back as `after`. With `survey`, which dumps of a folder refer to a GUID.

after.description: The `next` of the page before, to go on from where it stopped.

document.description: The document's id from `documents`. Default: the focused one.

forms.description: Which forms of `address` to search: "bus", "file", "region". Default all three.

limit.description: The most items one page holds — a ceiling: a page stops sooner when the answer would pass the size bound, and says so with `truncated: "size"`. Default 50, at most 200.

relative_to.description: What `address` counts from: the file (default) or the BIOS region.

name: refs
title: Find references to an address or a GUID

description: Read a module's stored code analysis. The module is the Code panel or tab given as `document`; or a PE32/TE image `node` of a dump (`code_modules` lists the ones with an analysis), its bytes hashed to find the analysis; or a `module` SHA-256, read from the store alone. No panel needs to be open. `what` picks the list (default "functions"): "functions"; one function's "instructions" or decompiled "c"; a function's callers and callees ("references"); the instructions that "uses" an address — who calls a function, jumps to a label, or reads a global or a string; "strings"; "symbols", the named data — GUIDs, service tables, interfaces; or "post_codes", the values written to port 0x80 (what a POST card shows), each at the call that supplies it, with the functions it passes through (`via`) — `search` narrows by value — and, last, the writes whose value or port the code does not say (`unresolved`). A function's `name_source` says where its name came from: DEFAULT is Ghidra's FUN_ placeholder, ANALYSIS a name the UEFI pass read from the module (`name_reason` says from what), IMPORTED the image's own. Addresses come twice: `entry`/`address` is Ghidra's virtual address, `offset` the same byte's offset in the module, the number the hex view shows (none when read by `module` alone). To show the person a function, `open_code`; to leave a note on it, `annotate` with `function`. These are stored observations, not a live disassembly; the C is Ghidra's reading of the instructions, not the source.

document.description: A Code panel or tab, or the dump the module is in. Default: the focused one.

function.description: A function name or Ghidra entry address, for "instructions", "c" and "references".

limit.description: The most items one page holds — a ceiling: a page stops sooner when the answer would pass the size bound, and says so with `truncated: "size"`. Default 200, at most 500.

module.description: Or the module by its bytes' SHA-256, read from the store without a dump.

node.description: The module's PE32/TE image node in the dump, e.g. "0.6.4.0.0.205.2" — from `code_modules`.

recipe.description: With `module`: which analysis, when there are several. Default: the newest.

search.description: A word to narrow functions, strings or symbols by.

name: code_query
title: Read a module's code analysis

description: The PE32/TE modules of a dump that have a stored code analysis: their image `node`, name, the analyses (`recipes`, newest first) and how many functions the newest found. The modules are found by their bytes — the same module in another dump has the same analysis — including those inside compressed sections, which are opened for it: seconds on a large image the first time. Read one with `code_query`, show it with `open_code`.

document.description: The dump. Default: the focused one.

name: code_modules
title: List a dump's analyzed modules

description: Opens the Code panel of a module — its functions, ASM and C beside its bytes — over the dump, at a `function` or an instruction `address` when given, and brings it forward: what the person's Open with Code does. Give the dump `document` and the image `node` (`code_modules`), or a Code panel as `document` to move it to another place. `view` chooses the side the reader lands on: `c` for the decompiled listing, `asm` for the assembly. A panel of the same module already open is raised rather than opened twice. Answers the panel's `document` id, which `code_query` reads.

address.description: Or an instruction's Ghidra address to open at.

document.description: The dump, or a Code panel. Default: the focused one.

function.description: A function name or Ghidra entry address to open at.

node.description: The module's PE32/TE image node in the dump.

view.description: Which side to show: "c" for the decompiled listing, "asm" for the assembly. Default: the panel keeps the side it has.

name: open_code
title: Open a module's code

description: The modules that have a kept Ghidra project: `module` (SHA-256), `name`, whether an owner is `running`, whether the project holds a review (`reviewed`), and its last publish (`published`: artifact, recipe, revision).
name: ghidra_modules
title: List the modules kept in Ghidra

description: Opens a module for a review in Ghidra and answers its owner's `hello`: program, functions, unpublished changes. Give the PE32/TE image `node` of a dump (`uefi_find` with `name: "PE32 image"` or `"TE image"` lists them) and its `document`: its bytes go to Ghidra, whose project is made the first time — seconds for a PEIM, a minute for a large DXE driver. A module seen before opens by `module`, the SHA-256 the answer gives. Ghidra is the analysis server's when Settings ▸ Code Analysis names one, and this Mac's own otherwise. Then read, rename, type and comment with the other `ghidra_` tools and `ghidra_publish`: every ByteRipper reading shows the result. A review aims at C that reads like source — enums for constants, structures for pointer walks, comments a source would have; the MCP instructions spell the rules out.

document.description: The dump the node is in. Default: the focused one.

module.description: Or a module already opened, by its SHA-256.

name.description: What to call the module. Default: the file it is in.

node.description: The PE32 or TE image node, e.g. "0.6.4.0.0.199.3".

name: ghidra_open
title: Open a module in Ghidra

description: The module's functions as Ghidra holds them now: entry, name, name_source, size, signature. `name_contains` and `name_source` (a Ghidra source such as USER_DEFINED) narrow the list, `address_from`/`address_to` narrow it by entry. `filter: "unfinished"` keeps what a review has not passed — a parameter or a local Ghidra still names itself or holds as `undefined`, or no plate comment — each with `leftovers`, and `summary` says how many of how many; that filter decompiles every function, so it is slow on a large module. Paged by `offset` and `limit`; `next` says where the next page starts.

address_from.description: Only functions whose entry is at or after this address.

address_to.description: Only functions whose entry is at or before this address.

filter.description: Only the functions a review has not passed.

limit.description: The most items one page holds — a ceiling: a page stops sooner when the answer would pass the size bound, and says so with `truncated: "size"`. Default 200, at most 1000.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

name_contains.description: Only functions whose name holds this text.

name_source.description: Only functions from this Ghidra source: DEFAULT, ANALYSIS, IMPORTED, USER_DEFINED.

name: ghidra_functions
title: List a module's functions

description: One function as Ghidra holds it now: its signature, its parameters and locals with their `storage` and `first_use` (what `ghidra_rename_variable` names a local by), its plate comment, what is left to name (`leftovers`), and its decompiled C — fresh after every write, ahead of what the app shows until a publish. `summary: true` leaves the C and the equates out, for walking a module without its text.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

summary.description: Leave out the decompiled C and the equates: signature, parameters, locals, plate, leftovers.

name: ghidra_function
title: Read one function

description: The instructions of the function at `address`, with their bytes, references and the names of their constants (`equates`). A large function comes in pages: `limit` instructions from `from`; `next` is the address to pass as `from` for the rest.

from.description: The first instruction of the page. Default: the function's first.

limit.description: The most instructions in the page. Default: all.

module.description: The module: the SHA-256 of its bytes, as `ghidra_modules` lists it.

name: ghidra_disassembly

The written bytes show red until the person saves, and the dump scrolls to them. `expect` makes the write conditional: the bytes there now must be these, or nothing is written and the answer says what is there. Overwrites only: a range past the end of the other file is refused, never grown. One undo step in the receiving file, named by `label`; the copied bytes show red until the person saves, and its pane scrolls to them. description: Puts a part's bytes back into the document it was opened from — File ▸ Update in Parent. The part's codec says how: a copy goes back as it is, a decompressed body is compressed again and the image laid out around it, a decoded block is encoded again with its checksum. One undo step in the parent; the parent's bytes show red until the person saves, and the parent is shown where they landed. A part with nothing new answers `updated: false`. Refused, with nothing written: when the parent is closed or read-only; when the codec cannot put the bytes back (a part whose length changed, a body that no longer fits once compressed — the answer gives the codec's reason); when the parent changed while the update was worked out (call again); and when the bytes the part came from have changed in the parent since it was opened — then ask the person, and call again with `overwrite_changed_source: true` only if they agree. A refusal that is a caution rather than an impossibility — a part of the BIOS image an AMD PSP decompresses itself, which the PSP may not accept once compressed again — says so: then explain the risk to the person, and call again with `update_anyway: true` only if they agree. Needs the person's permission — Settings ▸ Agent, "Let agents edit open files". Never saves.

description: Judges by their bytes the nodes the parser cannot name — Padding (the flash map's Unused, Unknown and named areas among them) and Raw files and sections — under `node` (default: the BIOS region), in address order. A node its children divide is replaced by them; one whose only child covers it whole stays, naming the child as `inner`. Each: `node`, `name`, `type`, `subtype`, `guid`, `start`, `end`, `size`; `fill` (the share of 0xFF and 0x00 bytes), `first_nonfill` and `last_nonfill` (the first and the last other byte); `class` — `empty` (at least 99% fill), `text` (most of the other bytes are ASCII or UTF-16LE strings of 4 characters or more), `code` (x86-64 instructions, by a heuristic: frequent REX.W moves, calls and returns, or a PE image), else `data`; and up to five `strings` with their addresses. The bytes themselves are never answered: `read` or `uefi_node_data` read them. An area whose name in the flash map says MSDM, Password or Key gives its class and sizes, no strings, and `redacted: true`. `kinds` picks the node types (the Type or Subtype column), default Padding and Raw; `min_size` leaves out smaller nodes. Pages: `limit`, `after` as in `uefi_find`. With `survey`, the same area across a folder of dumps.

description: The image's DMI areas — where the firmware keeps the board's identity: serial numbers, UUID, model — as the UEFI Structure panel's DMI button finds them. It opens every container in the file, but no compressed section. Each area: `layout` ("Lenovo DMI store", "GPNV store", "Acer DMI", "Panasonic DMI" — the Type column calls these Padding — or "HP DMI", a VSS entry that may be one the store marks deleted, as most HP boards keep it, or "Apple DMI", a SysF store), its node as `uefi_tree` gives it (`id`, `label`, `link`, `start`, `end`, `encoded` for an XORed LENV block), `size`, `path`, and the panel's `fields` and `tables` for it; `uefi_node` on its children reads further, `uefi_node_data` reads the bytes. The parser finds a DMI area only by its algorithms for the dump layouts it knows: Lenovo's DMI store (an LDBG change log and two LENV blocks), AMI's GPNV store as ASUS writes it, Acer's 8 KiB DMI area, Panasonic's DMI area (a MEI_ header, a directory and records), and HP's HP_MUD variable in the main VSS2 store, with BuildId, FactoryConfig (the feature byte) and HP_TAGS (the asset tracking number) beside it — what HP's BCU reports, and Apple's SysF store of the Mac's serial number (ssn), configuration code (hwc) and sales order number (son), with the board's serial read from the names of its calibration variables. An area that is not found is not therefore absent from the dump: it may be in a layout the parser does not know, or a known one that is damaged, wiped or moved so its checks fail. So an empty `areas` means only that the parser recognised none — say so to the person, never that the dump has no DMI; `region_scan` judges the nameless areas by their bytes, which is where to look next. With `survey`, group a folder of dumps by "total" or "areas.0.layout" — the whole answer holds each board's own serials, so no two dumps would share a group.

description: The NVRAM variables the image keeps, from every VSS, VSS2, NVAR, Dell DVAR and GPNV store — those inside compressed sections too, so the first call on a large image takes a few seconds. `stores` lists the stores the rows are in, with how many variables each holds. One row per variable: the copy that stands for it now. `copies` above 1 says the store still keeps earlier values (`uefi_node` on the entry lists them); `deleted: true` is a variable the store no longer holds, listed only with `deleted`. Each row: name, GUID, the store's and the entry's node ids, the value's bytes (`start`, `end`, `size`), and `value` — the value read as its type (a number, text, a boot option, a device path, a signature list) or as hex when it is short. Other stores (EVSA, Apple SysF, flash maps) are in `uefi_tree`. Pages: `limit` is a ceiling — a page also stops before the answer passes the size bound and then says `truncated: "size"`; pass `next` back as `after` until it is null. `total` counts every row. A row too large alone comes without its `value`, marked `truncated: "item"`; `read` its bytes.

description: Reads a node's bytes as `read` reads a document's — rows of 16 with their address, text, or integers — at addresses inside the node's `part` (`body` by default, `header`, or `all`), from 0. Works for a node inside a compressed section too, which has no file address and which `read` cannot reach: its bytes are what the tree decompressed it to, and `source` says which compressed section in the file they came out of. For a compressed section itself, part `decompressed` is what it decompresses to — the buffer its children are in. `size` is the whole part's, to read on by `offset`; at most 4096 bytes at a time. A node of the file gives `file_start` as well: its bytes are the document's at that address, unsaved edits included, and `read`, `reveal` and `write` work there. `find_bytes` with `node` searches the node and everything decompressed or decoded under it.

description: Sets the files of the ME file systems of two documents side by side — `document` and `against` — by what each volume calls them (an MFS file's index, an EFS file's file ID) and by what they hold, not by address. An MFS volume moves its pages to spread the wear, so one machine's two dumps keep the same file in different places, and `diff` over the MFS partition mostly finds pages moved; this says which files changed. Content is compared without the Integrity table a protected file ends with; that table changes whenever the engine writes the file again, so it is reported apart (`integrity_differs`). Answers `counts` (same — and of those, `moved` and `rewritten` — different, only in one, incomplete), the files that differ with both sizes and how many content bytes differ, and the files only in one dump. `name` is the file table's path or name where it gives one. A volume that could not be read on either side is under `not_compared` with the reason, and its files are not listed as missing. `incomplete` is a file whose chain of chunks broke off, so what it holds is not known whole. With `extents`, each listed file says where it is stored in each dump: the stretches in the file's own order, which `read` reads back. Pages: the lists are one sequence — `different`, `only_in_document`, `only_in_against`, `incomplete` — and `limit` is the most items of it on one page, a ceiling: a page also stops before the answer passes the size bound and then says `truncated: "size"`. Pass `next` back as `after` until it is null; `counts` are of the whole comparison. A file whose extents are too many for one answer lists the first of them, marked `truncated: "item"`; `me_tree` on the file lists them. `encrypted` is the file table's flag: an encrypted file the engine wrote again with a new nonce differs in nearly every byte, so for it `different` says it was written, not that what it holds changed.

description: Sets the NVRAM variables of two documents side by side — `document` and `against` — by name and GUID, not by address, so two dumps of different boards or BIOS versions compare as well as two of one board. A name and GUID kept twice in an image (live and default stores) is paired by which time it is met. Answers the variables only in one of them, those whose values differ — with both sizes, the bytes that differ as offsets into the value, and both values read as their type — and how many are the same. Variables a store no longer holds are left out. `survey` with this tool and a fixed `against` compares a folder of dumps with one. Pages: the three lists are one sequence — `changed`, then `only_in_document`, then `only_in_against` — and `limit` is the most items of it on one page, a ceiling: a page also stops before the answer passes the size bound and then says `truncated: "size"`. Pass `next` back as `after` until it is null; `counts` and `same` are of the whole comparison. A changed variable too large alone comes without its values, marked `truncated: "item"`.
